title: Probing Quantum Anomalous Hall Transport Under Microwave Irradiation Using a Topological Circulator
authors: Athul Ashok, Frank Jin, Nick Du, Luis A. Martinez, Jenny Zhou, Sean O'Kelley, Zachary J. -R. Espley, Gang Qiu, Kang L. Wang, Dong-Xia Qu
abstract: Edge magnetoplasmons (EMPs) provide a platform for probing chiral charge dynamics and nonreciprocal microwave transport in topological quantum materials. However, detecting small perturbations to EMP propagation remains challenging because their signatures in conventional microwave scattering measurements can be weak. Here, we investigate microwave-photon-induced perturbations of EMP transport using a quantum anomalous Hall topological circulator. Pump--probe measurements reveal a strongly frequency-selective response: while microwave irradiation substantially modifies the EMP transmission at several pump frequencies, the transmission remains nearly unchanged at selected frequencies, including 4 and 7 GHz. We further exploit the non-Hermitian mode hybridization of the coupled EMP-resonator system to probe the response near an exceptional point (EP). The pump-induced change in transmission magnitude near the EP is approximately twice that observed away from the EP, demonstrating an enhanced microwave response to perturbations. These results reveal the interplay among chiral EMP transport, microwave-photon-induced perturbations, and non-Hermitian dynamics, and demonstrate the potential of topological circulators as a promising platform for enhanced microwave spectroscopy and sensing.
summary: This work demonstrates the use of a topological circulator to probe chiral edge magnetoplasmon transport using microwave-photon interactions. By analyzing the system near an exceptional point, the researchers achieved a quantitative enhancement of the microwave response to perturbations. This confirms the potential of such topological structures for highly sensitive microwave spectroscopy.
main_problem: The study investigates how microwave irradiation perturbs the transport of chiral edge magnetoplasmons (EMPs) in topological quantum materials.
main_result: The system exhibits a strongly enhanced microwave response near an exceptional point (EP), where the pump-induced change in transmission magnitude is approximately twice that observed away from the EP.
method: The research uses pump-probe microwave measurements on a topological circulator coupled to LC resonators, analyzing the resulting non-Hermitian mode hybridization.
model_or_system: The physical system is a Quantum Anomalous Hall (QAH) topological circulator coupled to LC resonators, modeled by an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian describing coupled EMP-resonator dynamics.
key_observables: Nonreciprocal microwave transmission contrast, power-dependent hybridization splitting, and the change in transmission magnitude ($\vert S_{32} \vert$) as a function of pump power.
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($g_f \approx 39.66$ MHz), operating frequencies (e.g., 642.3 MHz near EP), and the dependence on pump power.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the system using an effective non-Hermitian coupled-mode model and approximating frequency variations linearly with input power.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the pump-probe measurement setup, power-dependent microwave transmission responses showing frequency selectivity, and the hybridization spectrum mapping the nonreciprocal contrast.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical platform and the challenge of measurement sensitivity, to developing the coupled-mode Hamiltonian, presenting the pump-probe measurements, and finally quantifying the enhanced response near the EP.
why_interesting: The explicit use of non-Hermitian physics, exceptional points, and microwave-induced perturbations provides a rich platform for studying open quantum systems dynamics, which is highly relevant to AMO and quantum optics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Pump–probe measurement configuration for the topolog- ical circulator. A continuous-wave pump generated by the vector signal generator (Keysight N5182B MXG) is applied to Port 1 (P1). The Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC board with the Quantum Instrumenta- tion Control Kit (QICK) digital-to-analog converter (DAC) supplies the probe signal to Port 2 (P2) through a programmable attenuator (RCDAT), which sets the probe power incident on the device. The resulting transmission is collected at Port 3 (P3), amplified by a low- noise amplifier (LNA), and digitized by the RFSoC/QICK analog-to- digital converter (ADC).

FIG. 2. Transmission response of the circulator as a function of input power. (a)–(c) Power-dependent microwave transmission responses |S31|, |S32|, and |S32|−|S31| for the 100µm-radius circulator coupled to LC resonators. The signal is excited from ports 1 and 2, and measured at port 3. (d)–(f) Frequency line cuts from panels (a), (b), and (c) at an input power of P = −68 dBm. The insets in (d) and (e) show schematic device structures illustrating anticlockwise EMP transport from Port 1 to Port 3 and from Port 2 to Port 3, respectively.

FIG. 3. Power-dependent hybridization of the LC and EMP modes. Color map of the nonreciprocal transmission contrast, |S31| −|S32|, as a function of frequency and input power. The ex- tracted lower- and upper-frequency resonance branches are indicated by blue and orange circles, respectively, while the dashed curves show a fit to the two-mode coupled-resonator model.

FIG. 4. Microwave transmission spectra between 500 and 700 MHz under various pump powers. A continuous-wave pump signal from the MXG is injected through Port 1, with the pump frequency varied from 1 to 9 GHz over a range of power levels. The transmission spectra are measured using the RFSoC/QICK setup by applying a 2.2 µs-long excitation pulse to Port 2 and measuring the transmitted signal at Port 3, as shown in the inset of (a). The two dashed lines mark the frequencies at 551.5 and 642.3 MHz.

FIG. 5. Pump-power dependence of the transmission response at two probe frequencies. Transmission magnitude |S32| as a function of pump power for pump frequencies from 1 to 9 GHz, measured at probe frequencies of 551.5 MHz (solid lines) and 642.3 MHz (dashed lines). The 642.3 MHz traces are vertically offset by −6 dB for clar- ity. The response at 642.3 MHz, near the exceptional point, exhibits a substantially stronger pump-power dependence for several pump frequencies than the response at 551.5 MHz, away from the excep- tional point, while selected pump frequencies show comparatively weak perturbation.
